headline: Highest risk is capability conflict: Aider can write/commit to a shared git repo while awesome-selfhosted is a non-runnable knowledge list, so prompt-injection, leakage, and cascading-error risks are limited.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: Aider can read/write repo files and auto-commit, so malicious content in shared files could influence its prompts. awesome-selfhosted is not runnable and has no I/O surfaces, so the interaction is mostly one-way and requires manual file bridging rather than a live shared channel.
conditions: IF the operator copies attacker-controlled text from the repo into Aider prompts, injection becomes plausible.
IF awesome-selfhosted is converted into a live agent with file access, the pathway broadens.
mitigations: Review repo content before pasting into prompts.
Keep Aider on a separate working tree from untrusted content.
Use commit diffs as the only input to downstream review.
requires-engineering: add provenance labels to imported text.

B_data_leakage.rationale: Aider touches source code and git history and can use broad network egress, but awesome-selfhosted has no data classes or I/O surfaces and is not runnable. There is no documented shared workspace or outbound flow from B, so leakage is limited to manual exposure of repo contents through Aider.
conditions: IF the shared repo contains secrets or private source code, Aider can expose them through its networked model calls.
IF awesome-selfhosted is replaced with a runnable agent that reads the same workspace, leakage risk increases.
mitigations: Remove secrets from the repo before use.
Restrict Aider to a sanitized branch.
Disable or review networked model calls for sensitive files.
requires-engineering: add secret-scanning pre-commit hooks.

C_capability_conflict.rationale: Aider has filesystem write and git-state modification, but awesome-selfhosted is non-runnable and has no write capabilities. The pair does not show overlapping mutable-resource access, so direct conflict is unlikely unless the operator repurposes awesome-selfhosted into an active writer.
conditions: IF another process writes the same git repo concurrently, Aider can race on commits.
IF awesome-selfhosted is wrapped into a tool-using agent with write access, conflict risk rises.
mitigations: Use one writer per repo at a time.
Stash or commit before switching tasks.
Lock the working tree during automated edits.
requires-engineering: add repo-level mutexing.

D_cascading_error.rationale: Aider can generate edits and commits, but awesome-selfhosted is a static knowledge resource, not an action-taking agent. There is no evidence that B consumes A's output as authoritative or performs downstream actions, so cascading failure is mostly limited to human misuse of generated diffs.
conditions: IF a human treats Aider's generated patch as authoritative without review, errors can propagate.
IF awesome-selfhosted is transformed into an automated executor, downstream impact increases.
mitigations: Require human review of every diff.
Run tests before merge.
Limit Aider to small, isolated changes.
requires-engineering: add automated validation gates.

E_compliance.rationale: Aider handles source code, git history, and provider API keys, while awesome-selfhosted has no declared data classes or residency/compliance obligations. No mismatch is documented, so compliance risk is limited to operator handling of code secrets rather than a pairwise policy conflict.
conditions: IF the repo contains regulated data or secrets, Aider's handling may create policy obligations.
IF awesome-selfhosted is assigned regulated data classes later, a residency or retention mismatch could emerge.
mitigations: Keep regulated data out of the repo.
Rotate any exposed API keys.
Document retention rules for generated patches.
requires-engineering: map data classes to approved processors.
